description_ru: Биография Николы Теслы: от лихорадочных видений в Смиляне до войны токов, Ниагарского водопада и одинокой смерти в нью-йоркском отеле.
text:
Nikola Tesla was born at midnight, according to family legend, during a violent electrical storm, and the midwife is supposed to have muttered that the child would be a child of darkness. His mother, Đuka, replied with fine presence of mind that he would be a child of light. The anecdote is almost certainly embroidered, but it has survived because it fits so tidily. Tesla was born on the tenth of July 1856, in the village of Smiljan, then part of the Austrian Empire and now in Croatia, to a Serbian family. His father, Milutin, was an Orthodox priest; his mother, though unlettered, was a gifted inventor of household gadgets.

The boy possessed a mind that seemed to run a theatre without his permission. From early childhood he was assailed by blinding flashes of light and by vivid images that appeared before his eyes in response to a word, so that, on hearing the name of an object, he could not help seeing it. He later learned to harness the faculty, building and testing entire machines in his head, and claimed that the devices, when finally assembled, worked exactly as he had imagined. It was a gift, but also a form of torment, and it never really left him.

A tragedy marked his youth. His older brother Dane, a prodigy whom the family expected to outshine them all, died after a fall from a horse, and the parents' grief was so deep that Nikola felt he could never live up to the memory. He fell ill with cholera at seventeen, lingered at death's door for nine months, and extracted from his father a promise that, if he recovered, he would be allowed to study engineering rather than enter the priesthood. He recovered, and his father kept his word.

At the Polytechnic in Graz he developed a passion for alternating current and a certain contempt for his professor, who insisted that the commutator in a direct-current motor could not be removed. Tesla thought it could. He left without a degree, wandered to Prague, worked for a telephone company in Budapest and, one afternoon in 1882, strolling through a city park and reciting lines from Goethe's Faust, saw in a flash the whole design of a motor driven by a rotating magnetic field. He seized a stick and sketched the diagram in the sand, as one might sketch a treasure map.

In 1884 he sailed to New York, carrying, as he later told it, four cents, a book of his own poems and a letter of introduction to Thomas Edison. He was hired at once, put to work on repairing and improving Edison's direct-current dynamos, and, he said, promised a fee of fifty thousand dollars if he could improve them. When he delivered, Edison laughed and told him that he did not understand American humour. Tesla resigned, dug ditches for a living for a while, and then secured backers for a company of his own.

The consequences were industrial. George Westinghouse, an entrepreneur with a bold imagination, purchased Tesla's patents for an alternating-current system, and the two found themselves in a ferocious commercial contest, nicknamed the War of the Currents, against Edison, who denounced alternating current as lethal and organised public electrocutions of stray animals to prove it. Direct current, however, could not be sent far without ruinous losses. In 1893 the Chicago World's Fair was illuminated by Westinghouse's alternating current, and in 1895 a power station at Niagara Falls began to send electricity to Buffalo, vindicating Tesla.

His inventiveness was relentless. He devised the Tesla coil, a resonant transformer capable of producing spectacular lightning, demonstrated wireless lighting by illuminating gas-filled tubes without wires, controlled a small boat by radio waves in front of an astonished audience at Madison Square Garden, and sketched designs for a bladeless turbine. In 1899 he moved to Colorado Springs, where he generated artificial lightning bolts several metres long and persuaded himself that he had received signals from another planet.

Success, however, did not make him wise with money. He had a lordly generosity and a disdain for contracts. When Westinghouse, on the edge of ruin, begged him to waive a royalty on every horsepower sold, Tesla magnanimously tore up the agreement, forgoing a fortune that would probably have made him one of the richest men in the world. Later, with funds from the financier J. P. Morgan, he began building a colossal tower at Wardenclyffe, on Long Island, meant to transmit messages and power across the planet without wires.

The tower was never finished. Morgan declined to provide further capital, partly because Guglielmo Marconi had sent a radio signal across the Atlantic first, using, as it happened, several of Tesla's patented ideas, and partly because a system that provided free energy to everyone offered investors little prospect of profit. The tower was demolished in 1917, to pay a hotel debt. Marconi received the Nobel Prize in 1909; it was only in 1943, a few months after Tesla's death, that the Supreme Court restored the priority of his basic radio patents.

His later years grew increasingly eccentric. He lived in a succession of New York hotels, fed pigeons in the park, and developed a particular affection for one white bird, declaring that he had loved her as a man loves a woman. He was obsessed with the number three, washed his hands compulsively, and used eighteen napkins to polish his silverware before every meal. He made grand announcements to journalists about death rays and interplanetary communication, and a gullible public, accustomed to his past miracles, listened with respect.

He died alone in Room 3327 of the Hotel New Yorker, on the seventh of January 1943, aged eighty-six, practically penniless. Yet the verdict of history has been generous. In 1960 the international unit of magnetic flux density was named the tesla, and alternating current continues to power almost every home in the world. The child of light had, after all, lit the planet, though he was never allowed to profit from it, a fate that bitterly justifies his own wry remark that the present is theirs, but the future is mine.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Губы вытянуты трубочкой, нижняя губа не касается зубов; сравните с английским v, где касание есть.
Нижняя губа касается верхних зубов, голос включён; не оглушайте в «ф».
Не оглушайте конечные звонкие согласные: d, b, g в конце слова звучат с голосом, как в слове «год», а не «гот».
Короткий, расслабленный гласный в центре рта, ближе к русскому «а» без напряжения губ.

questions.question: Where and when was Tesla born?
What did Tesla see in a park in Budapest in 1882?
questions.answer: The design of a rotating magnetic field motor.

questions.question: What was the War of the Currents?
questions.answer: The contest between Edison's direct current and Westinghouse's alternating current.

questions.question: Why did Tesla tear up his contract with Westinghouse?
questions.answer: To save Westinghouse from ruin by waiving his royalty.
